units.title: Fundamental Cloud Concepts
units.summary: Separate usage, responsibility boundaries, and failure scope to choose a cloud configuration that meets the requirements.
units.objective: Explain why a cloud configuration is selected by distinguishing usage, the layer under your responsibility, and the scope of failures.
explanation: In the cloud, you can use the resources you need only for the period you need them, but responsibility for managing capacity, configuration, and data remains.
By checking load mitigation, shared responsibility, and failure scope separately, you can explain the trade-offs between cost and availability.

sections.title: Prepare resources when needed and reassess the required amount
paragraphs: On-demand means using resources such as compute, storage, and networking when they are needed. Instead of fixing capacity for the maximum load from the outset, measure actual usage and adjust capacity.

Scale-out means increasing the number of instances, scale-in means decreasing it, and scale-up means increasing the capability of one instance. The ability to change something and changing it automatically are different, so automation requires conditions and limits.
Stopping compute resources does not necessarily eliminate charges for retained disks or stored data. Check the purpose, retention period, and cost for each resource.

example.scenario: Run an internal aggregation in the cloud that is small on weekdays and increases only at the end of the month.
steps: Measure the processing volume on weekdays.
Increase compute capacity only at the end of the month.
After processing, reduce unnecessary compute resources and retain the data that is needed.
example.outcome: This makes it possible to assess peak handling and normal-period costs separately.

misconception.claim: Moving to the cloud will reduce costs without any action.
misconception.correction: Because unused compute resources, storage, and data transfer may still incur charges, reassess usage and retained resources.

takeaways: Distinguish between being able to use resources when needed and automatic adjustment.
Check costs by factor, such as compute, storage, and data transfer.

sections.title: What AWS manages and what you must protect yourself
paragraphs: The shared responsibility model defines the boundary between the infrastructure AWS manages and the settings and data managed by the customer.
AWS manages facilities, physical equipment, and the service infrastructure. Customers manage data exposure, permissions, and network settings.
For EC2, customers update the guest OS and installed applications. For S3, customers do not manage the OS, but they verify data access permissions.

example.scenario: A vulnerable dependency library was found in an EC2 web application.
steps: Identify that the target is an application on the guest OS, not the physical infrastructure.
Create an update plan and perform operational checks on the customer side.
Also check permissions and exposure.
example.outcome: Do not confuse AWS physical protection with customer maintenance of the OS and applications.

misconception.claim: All resources on AWS are updated by AWS.
misconception.correction: Responsibility differs by service and layer; the EC2 guest OS and customer settings remain the customer’s responsibility.

takeaways: Identify the service name and the layer involved in the problem.
Consider the physical infrastructure, OS, application, and data permissions separately.

sections.title: Separate failure scope using Regions and AZs
paragraphs: A Region is a geographic unit where resources are placed. An AZ is an isolated location within a Region, and resources in the same AZ may share a common failure scope.

Increasing the number of instances within the same AZ can protect against a single-instance failure, but it does not separate the failure scope of the entire AZ. Distributing resources across different AZs separates the failure scopes.
Switching Regions in the console does not automatically move or replicate existing resources. Replication to another Region requires service-specific configuration.

example.scenario: Assume a failure in which two instances in the same AZ stop at the same time.
steps: Distinguish a single-instance failure from an AZ failure.
Place the required processing in another AZ as well.
Check the remaining capacity and reachability of dependent data.
example.outcome: This makes it possible to evaluate availability by separating failure domains, not merely by counting instances.

misconception.claim: Adding AZs automatically replicates resources to another Region.
misconception.correction: AZ distribution and cross-Region replication are separate designs and configurations.

takeaways: An AZ is a failure-isolation unit within a Region.
Placement in different AZs alone does not guarantee remaining capacity or data availability.

sections.title: Compare load, failures, and cost separately
paragraphs: Load mitigation is a design that secures the required processing capacity; failure mitigation is a design that separates resources from a common failure scope. Because the objectives differ, simply increasing the number of instances does not satisfy both.

If the requirement is to continue operating when one AZ stops, compare the cost of redundancy across AZs, the remaining capacity, and the reachability of dependencies. If the high load is brief, also compare an option that increases capacity only for that period.
Choose a configuration based not only on the lowest price, but also on who is affected, how long they can wait, and what risks remain.

example.scenario: High load occurs for only one hour per month, and processing must continue after one AZ stops.
steps: Compare capacity options for the peak period.
Compare the cost and effect of redundancy across AZs.
Verify the remaining processing volume after an AZ stops.
example.outcome: Explain the trade-offs among load, availability, and cost.

misconception.claim: Placing one high-performance instance makes the system more resilient to an AZ failure.
misconception.correction: Capacity and failure scope are separate; an AZ failure requires distribution across locations.

takeaways: Use load, failure, and cost as separate decision criteria.
Do not choose the cheapest configuration if it does not meet the requirements.

explanation: Rather than deciding from the service name, break down who executes what and when, and how the data should be stored and searched.
An execution environment, object storage, attached disks, relational searches, and key-centered searches are separate responsibilities.

sections.title: Compute: Who manages the execution environment
paragraphs: EC2 is a virtual server that lets users manage the OS and installed software. It is a candidate for comparison when resident software, long-running processes, or OS configuration are requirements.
Lambda is a service that runs code in response to events, and users do not manage the server OS. Select it after checking processing time, concurrency, and the event trigger.

example.scenario: Run a short image-resizing process only when an image arrives in S3.
steps: Use the arrival event as the execution trigger.
Check Lambda's processing time and retries.
Compare it with EC2 if OS-resident software is required.
example.outcome: Distinguish event-driven processing from processing that requires OS management.

misconception.claim: S3 does not execute a conversion command just because a file is placed in S3.
misconception.correction: S3 is a storage service. Assign conversion to an execution environment such as Lambda or EC2.

takeaways: Compare Lambda when event-driven processing can reduce OS management.
Compare EC2 when resident software or OS management is required.

sections.title: Storage: Object or attached disk
paragraphs: S3 is object storage that handles images, documents, and other data by key. It is suited to originals and outputs shared by name across multiple processes.
EBS is block storage attached to EC2 and is used for operating-system file systems and similar purposes. Lambda's temporary storage is not a persistent shared storage location.

example.scenario: Store the EC2 operating-system area separately from users' uploaded images.
steps: Use EBS as a candidate for the operating-system area.
Use an S3 object as a candidate for the image data.
Check the key, retention period, and access principal.
example.outcome: Do not confuse attached disks with shared objects.

misconception.claim: If you store all data in IAM, you can also manage access.
misconception.correction: IAM provides access control; it is not a storage location for images or documents.

takeaways: S3 provides object storage accessed by key.
EBS is block storage attached to EC2.

sections.title: Database: Choose Based on Queries
paragraphs: RDS is a service for operating relational databases, so compare table relationships, SQL, joins, and transactions.
DynamoDB is a key-value database where access patterns and key design are decided first. Confirm which keys will be used for reads and writes and whether the required queries fit.

example.scenario: Join customers, orders, and order items to produce a monthly summary.
steps: List the required joins and consistency requirements.
Compare the SQL requirements using RDS as a candidate.
If key-based access is central, also compare DynamoDB against the separate requirements.
example.outcome: Choose based on queries and operational requirements rather than the service name.

misconception.claim: DynamoDB can automatically optimize joins on arbitrary columns afterward.
misconception.correction: DynamoDB requires access patterns and key design to come first and does not assume arbitrary joins.

takeaways: Joins, SQL, and transactions are comparison criteria for RDS.
Key-based access and query patterns are comparison criteria for DynamoDB.

sections.title: Composition: Decompose Requirements into Roles
paragraphs: Even within a single feature, receiving, storing, transforming, and searching are different responsibilities. Compare the execution method, data shape, queries, and permission boundaries for each responsibility separately.
Assign services to roles—for example, save images in S3, invoke Lambda when an arrival event occurs, and register order information in RDS or DynamoDB.

misconception.claim: Choose one familiar service first and fit the requirements to it afterward.
misconception.correction: First decompose the responsibilities for processing, storage, and search, then choose a combination that meets the requirements.

takeaways: Treat receiving, storing, transforming, and searching as separate responsibilities.
Check service selection and permission boundaries together.

units.title: Authentication and Authorization
units.summary: Distinguish who performs an operation, what is permitted, and who can assume a role to make IAM decisions.
units.objective: Distinguish authentication, authorization, IAM roles, and least privilege when deciding how to configure access.
explanation: Authentication verifies an identity; authorization determines what that identity can do with a resource.
A role's trust policy defines who can assume it, while its permissions policy defines what can be done after assuming it. An explicit Deny takes precedence over an Allow.

sections.title: Authentication and authorization are separate questions
paragraphs: Authentication verifies who the entity sending the request is. Passwords and multi-factor authentication strengthen verification of the entity.

Authorization determines whether a verified entity can perform a specific action on a resource. If an S3 operation returns AccessDenied after successful sign-in, check the authorization principal, action, resource, and policies.

example.scenario: The user signed in successfully, but GetObject on a specific bucket was denied.
steps: Separate successful authentication from denied authorization.
Identify the requested action and target resource.
Evaluate the applicable Allow, Deny, and condition.
example.outcome: You can investigate the denial layer without masking an authorization problem through password changes or public-access settings.

misconception.claim: Passing multi-factor authentication allows access to every bucket.
misconception.correction: Strengthening authentication does not automatically add permissions to authorization policies.

takeaways: Authentication answers who; authorization answers what can be done.
With AccessDenied, proceed to evaluate the request and policies.

sections.title: Principal and role-assumption conditions
paragraphs: A principal is an entity that requests AWS operations. People, applications running on EC2, and AWS services are examples.

IAM roles have trust policies and permissions policies. A trust policy specifies who can assume the role, while a permissions policy defines operations after assumption. STS issues temporary credentials.

example.scenario: Allow a batch to write to S3 for only 3 hours.
steps: Identify the entity running the batch.
Use the trust policy so that only that entity can assume the role.
Use the permissions policy to allow only the required bucket, prefix, and action.
example.outcome: You can separate entities and permissions without distributing long-term access keys.

misconception.claim: If a principal is written in a role’s trust policy, that principal can perform all AWS operations.
misconception.correction: A trust policy defines assumption conditions; operations after assumption are controlled separately by a permissions policy.

takeaways: A principal is not limited to a person; it also includes a running application.
Check the trust policy and permissions policy separately.

sections.title: Look at explicit Deny, not just Allow
paragraphs: IAM effective permissions are evaluated by combining the requested principal, action, resource, and condition with multiple applicable policies. Having one Allow does not establish permission.

An explicit Deny that applies to the request takes precedence over Allow. Check the scope of resource policy, identity policy, permissions boundary, Organizations controls, and other applicable policies.

example.scenario: There was an Allow for S3:GetObject, but the same target returned AccessDenied.
steps: Fix the actual principal, action, and resource.
Look for the applicable Deny and condition.
Evaluate the necessary Allow together with the boundary policies.
example.outcome: Do not work around the issue by allowing all operations; identify who is responsible for the denial.

misconception.claim: If you find an Allow, you can ignore Deny.
misconception.correction: An applicable explicit Deny takes precedence over Allow.

takeaways: Do not determine effective permissions from Allow alone.
Make the targets and conditions for Deny application specific.

sections.title: Least privilege and short-lived credentials
paragraphs: Least privilege is the principle of allowing a principal to perform only the actions needed for its work on the resources needed, under the required conditions and for the required period.
Credentials for an execution role are issued temporarily; long-term access keys are not placed in source code or shared configuration. Verify actual usage and reduce or update permissions.

steps: List the required GetObject and PutObject actions.
Limit the target bucket and prefix.
Associate the execution role with Lambda and do not store long-term keys.
example.outcome: You can reduce the impact of a leak and excessive permissions.

misconception.claim: When something does not work, grant administrator permissions for all AWS services.
misconception.correction: Identify the request and denial, then add only the required action, resource, and condition.

takeaways: Limit operations, targets, conditions, and periods.
Do not share a person’s keys with an application.

units.title: Data protection
units.summary: Distinguish between encryption in transit and at rest, KMS authorization, restore testing, and the retrieval and display of secrets.
units.objective: You can determine from specific conditions where protection is needed, who uses the key, whether restoration is possible, and how secrets may be exposed.
explanation: Verify separately the communication path and storage destination, KMS authorization, usability after restoration, and the path by which secrets are displayed, rather than considering only the encryption method.
units.example: Receive customer data over HTTPS, protect S3 with SSE-KMS, and operate restore testing with AWS Backup and least privilege in Secrets Manager.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish the protection boundaries for data in transit and data at rest, and verify S3 encryption settings.
Explain the relationship between the KMS key policy, IAM policy, grants, and the principals performing decryption.
Distinguish successful backups from recoverability, and validate the RTO/RPO through an actual restoration.
Separate secrets from code and logs, and minimize the permissions to retrieve the target secret.

sections.title: Protect data in transit and at rest separately
paragraphs: Data moving from the browser to the API and from the API to the storage destination is in transit. HTTPS protects HTTP with TLS, but protecting the communication path and protecting the storage destination are separate concerns.

Newly uploaded objects in Amazon S3 are encrypted at rest. The standard method is SSE-S3, which uses keys managed by S3. If a specified KMS key is required, verify the object's encryption method and that the execution role has permission to use that key.
In a design review, list the path, storage location, and access principal separately. Do not consider the review complete after checking only data in transit or only data at rest.

example.scenario: A customer uploads an invoice from a web page, and the API stores it in S3.
steps: Use HTTPS from the browser to the API.
Verify the path from the API to S3 and S3 default encryption.
If SSE-KMS is required, verify the actual object's encryption method, the specified KMS key, and the application's permission to use that key.
example.outcome: You can verify the separate protection boundaries for communication, storage, and key usage.

misconception.claim: If you upload using HTTPS, the organization-specified KMS key is also used for the file stored in S3.
misconception.correction: HTTPS protects the communication path. For objects stored in S3, verify the encryption method and KMS key through the S3 configuration or the specification made when writing the object.

takeaways: TLS protects data in transit.
Verify encryption at rest in the storage service.
Verify the encryption method and permission to use the key separately.

sections.title: Verify KMS keys and usage permissions separately
paragraphs: AWS KMS manages encryption keys. Merely specifying a key does not mean that any principal can perform encryption operations.

Whether a KMS key can be used is determined by the combination of the key policy, IAM policy, and grant. Even if IAM allows the operation, the permission is not effective unless the key policy permits that configuration.
During incident investigation, separate permission to read the target data from permission to decrypt it with the encryption key. Allow only the required principals and operations.

example.scenario: An application cannot read an S3 object encrypted with SSE-KMS.
steps: Identify the target object and execution role.
Check the S3 read permissions.
Check the decryption permissions in the KMS key policy and IAM policy.
example.outcome: You can distinguish and troubleshoot denials on the S3 side and the KMS side separately.

misconception.claim: If IAM policy allows kms:Decrypt, any KMS key can be decrypted.
misconception.correction: The target key's key policy and grants are also evaluated. Check permissions for both the key and the principal.

takeaways: The existence of a key does not grant permission to use it.
Check the key policy, IAM policy, and grant for the target key and principal.
Allow decryption operations only for the principals that need them.

sections.title: Verify backup success and restorability separately
paragraphs: A successful backup job indicates that recovery data was created, but it does not prove that the required state can be restored or that the application can be used.

Define how to verify the recovery point, restore target, RTO, RPO, data integrity, and application connectivity. Restore to an isolated environment and evaluate it, such as with AWS Backup restore testing.
A restore test does not overwrite production. Record the elapsed time, omissions, and reconnection procedure, and update the difference between the plan and the measured results.

example.scenario: The nightly backup of the order database succeeds, but the restore procedure has not been tested.
steps: Choose the recovery point and an isolated restore target.
Restore the database and verify its integrity and application connectivity.
Record the elapsed time and results and compare them with the RTO/RPO.
example.outcome: You can verify whether the system can return to an available state within the required time.

misconception.claim: A backup success notification completes the recovery plan.
misconception.correction: Actually verify the restore procedure, post-restore integrity, application connectivity, and elapsed time.

takeaways: Backup and restore verification are separate tasks.
Decide on the restore target and verification criteria first.
Perform a restore test in an isolated environment and compare it with the RTO/RPO.

sections.title: Separate secret storage, retrieval, and display
paragraphs: Passwords, API keys, and tokens are secrets. Placing them in plaintext in source code, configuration files, chats, or logs increases the number of viewers and copies.

Store secrets in AWS Secrets Manager, and have the application retrieve only the required secret using its execution role. Providing a storage location does not protect secrets if retrieval permissions are broad.
Do not output values in logs or error responses. Limit the target secret, and confirm that consumers can keep up after an update.

example.scenario: An application uses an external API token and records request information in logs during failures.
steps: Register the token in Secrets Manager and remove it from the code.
Allow the execution role to retrieve only the target secret.
Confirm that the value does not appear in logs or error displays.
example.outcome: Separating the storage location, retrieval principal, and display path limits the scope of a leak.

misconception.claim: Secrets are safe to log if they are stored in environment variables.
misconception.correction: Environment variables are also runtime secrets. Do not output their values in logs or errors, and limit the retrieval principal.

takeaways: Separate secrets from code and logs.
Minimize retrieval permissions for the target secret.
Confirm that values are not displayed or collected even after rotation.

questions.prompt: A developer gives the order application's execution role only the minimum permissions required for operations. The only secret the application needs to read is secret-a. Select one permission that should be granted.

choices.text: Allow retrieval of only secret-a
choices.explanation: This limits the target secret.

choices.text: Allow retrieval of all secrets
choices.explanation: This exposes unnecessary secrets.

choices.text: Always write retrieved values to the logs
choices.explanation: The logs become a path for leakage.

learning.reason: This limits the target secret.
learning.concept: Separate secrets from code and logs.

questions.title: Secret Rotation
questions.prompt: A person responsible for the order application verifies its behavior after rotating database credentials in AWS Secrets Manager. Select two methods that are incorrect for verification.

choices.text: Verify that the application can connect using the new value
choices.explanation: This verifies the consumer after the update.

choices.text: Output the old value to an incident log for comparison
choices.explanation: The old value is also a secret and must not be output.

choices.text: Change the execution role to an administrator role
choices.explanation: Excessive permissions are unnecessary.

choices.text: Verify that the value does not appear in logs or error responses
choices.explanation: This prevents leakage through display paths.

learning.reason: The old value is also a secret and must not be output. Excessive permissions are unnecessary.
learning.concept: Separate secrets from code and logs.

units.title: Troubleshooting Communication by Layer
units.summary: Treat names, IP addresses, ports, TLS, and HTTP as separate checkpoints, and narrow down failures using the evidence you need.
units.objective: Choose the next check from your observations without confusing the destination, service entry point, encryption, and HTTP processing.
explanation: Do not assume that a connection failure is simply a “network problem.” Instead, build up verified facts in order: name resolution, reachability to the destination IP, the port and listener, TLS, and HTTP.
units.example: When a user cannot connect to https://orders.example, check the DNS answer, the connection to TCP 443, the certificate name, and finally the HTTP response in that order.

learningObjectives.text: Be able to distinguish what an IP address and a port refer to.
Be able to compare TCP and UDP based on the delivery properties required.
TLS validation and the HTTP response can be treated as separate stages.
You can choose the next troubleshooting step based on the stage that has already been observed.

sections.title: IP addresses identify destinations; ports are service entry points.
paragraphs: An IP address represents a destination on the network to which packets are delivered. Even when multiple services exist on the same host or network interface, the IP address alone does not determine which service receives the traffic.

For TCP and UDP, port numbers distinguish service entry points. Security group rules also allow traffic by combining the protocol, port range, and source or destination. Port 443 is commonly used for HTTPS, but HTTPS is not necessarily on port 443.

Being able to SSH to an IP does not necessarily mean that you can connect to the web service at the same IP. For each service, check the port it uses, the settings along the path that allow that port, and whether the process is listening.

example.scenario: From an administration terminal, SSH to the same EC2 instance succeeds, but only the application's HTTPS fails.
steps: Confirm that the IP returned by DNS belongs to the expected EC2 instance.
If the design uses TCP 443, confirm permission and reachability from the source to port 443.
Confirm that the process on the EC2 instance is listening on that port and can present a certificate.
example.outcome: Do not judge all of HTTPS to be healthy based on successful SSH; investigate the service entry point and the upper layers separately.

misconception.claim: If you know an IP address, you can connect to any application on that host.
misconception.correction: An IP only identifies the destination. You can connect to the target service only when the protocol, port, permission, and service listener are all in place.

takeaways: IP addresses and ports are separate decision points.
The HTTPS port is determined by the configuration; do not assume only the default value.

sections.title: Choose between TCP and UDP based on where you place delivery responsibility.
paragraphs: TCP establishes a connection and provides a reliable byte stream using ordering and retransmission. It is used for applications such as web applications, where you do not want to handle missing requests or reordered data as-is.

UDP sends datagrams without establishing a connection. UDP itself does not guarantee delivery, ordering, or duplicate elimination, so design loss handling, ordering, and retransmission in the application when necessary.

Do not choose a method based only on “UDP is fast” or “TCP is safe.” First determine whether old data has value, whether loss is acceptable, and how waiting for retransmission affects the user experience.

example.scenario: Some packets of live audio arrive late.
steps: Decide whether it is valuable to play audio that arrives late and whether missing data needs to be compensated for.
Choose whether to delegate ordering and retransmission to the communication method or handle them in the application.
Evaluate the method using measured latency, loss, and user impact.
example.outcome: You can compare delivery guarantees and latency tolerance instead of choosing TCP/UDP by name.

misconception.claim: Choosing UDP always results in low latency, so ordering and loss do not need to be considered.
misconception.correction: UDP does not guarantee ordering or retransmission as a protocol. Even in a design that prioritizes low latency, you must decide where to compensate for loss.

takeaways: First write down the required delivery, ordering, and retransmission properties.
The application design is responsible for UDP's missing guarantees.

sections.title: TLS is the communication channel; HTTP handles application meaning.
paragraphs: TLS protects the communication channel between the client and server and validates items such as the certificate name, validity period, and trust chain. When TLS validation fails, the connection normally stops before an HTTP request is sent.

HTTP defines the meaning of request methods, URIs, status codes, and bodies. 404 is a response indicating that the target resource was not found as a result of processing an HTTP request. It is not at the same layer as a TLS failure or a DNS failure.

For an HTTPS incident, start with the observation you obtained. If the certificate name does not match, investigate TLS; if the result is 404, investigate HTTP routing or the application's resource, and do not repeatedly change a stage that has already succeeded.

example.scenario: The browser shows a certificate-name mismatch for orders.example and does not show an HTTP status code.
steps: Confirm that the name-resolution result and destination are as expected.
Check the certificate's SAN/CN, validity period, and trust chain.
Only after TLS validation succeeds, investigate the HTTP path and status code.
example.outcome: You can fix the certificate issue at the TLS stage instead of treating it as HTTP 404.

misconception.claim: If HTTPS returns 404, the TLS certificate is also broken.
misconception.correction: 404 is an HTTP response after TLS succeeds. Certificate validation and HTTP resource discovery are separate failure stages.

takeaways: TLS success does not mean HTTP success.
Investigate the stage after the last successfully observed stage.

sections.title: Choose the next stage based on evidence, not changes
paragraphs: In network diagnostics, record the name entered by the user, the DNS answer, the destination IP, the TCP connection to the port, TLS verification, and the HTTP response. While an earlier stage is failing, you cannot determine that a later stage is the cause.

Before broadening permissions or redeploying, choose an observation that can narrow the hypothesis to one possibility. For example, if the TCP connection is refused, check the destination IP, port, security group, and listener, and defer changes to the HTTP application.

After making a fix, observe again using the same name, source, port, and request. Do not stop after a single coincidental success; keep a record that disproves or supports the hypothesis made before the change.

example.scenario: Some users cannot connect to orders.example.
steps: Compare the DNS answers and destination IPs for each user.
Record TCP, TLS, and HTTP in sequence under the same source conditions.
After the minimum necessary change, test again under the same conditions to determine the scope of impact.
example.outcome: Avoid risky attempts such as opening all ports, and limit changes to the first stage that failed.

misconception.claim: If the cause is unknown, first open the security group completely to speed up troubleshooting.
misconception.correction: Opening everything adds new effects and makes the evidence ambiguous. Check the necessary source, protocol, and port in relation to the hypothesis.

takeaways: Treat the stages from DNS through HTTP as separate observation points.
After a fix, observe again under the same conditions.

questions.title: IP addresses and ports
questions.prompt: An operations administrator is reviewing a configuration in which SSH and HTTPS listen on the same IP address of a single EC2 instance. Choose one thing that cannot be distinguished by the destination IP address alone but can be distinguished by the port number.

choices.text: Which service on that IP address to deliver traffic to
choices.explanation: Correct. The port and protocol distinguish the service entry point.

choices.text: The packet’s destination on the network
choices.explanation: An IP address is used to identify the destination.

choices.text: The expiration date of the TLS certificate
choices.explanation: The certificate expiration date is part of TLS validation.

learning.concept: The scope distinguished by IP addresses and ports
learning.reason: The destination IP address specifies the communication destination, and the port number specifies which entry point at that destination to deliver the traffic to.

questions.title: Checking the service entry point
questions.prompt: An operations administrator is investigating why SSH provided by the same EC2 instance is reachable, but HTTPS on port 443 is not. After confirming that the address is reachable, choose one thing to investigate next.

choices.text: Permission for port 443 and service listening on that port
choices.explanation: Correct. IP reachability and permission and listening on a specific port must be checked separately.

choices.text: Only the S3 bucket name
choices.explanation: The bucket name does not indicate that the target service is listening on a port.

choices.text: Only KMS key rotation
choices.explanation: KMS key management is not a check of this TCP service entry point.

learning.concept: The destination port and listening service
learning.reason: Even with the same IP, the listening service for each individual service and communication permission for each port must be checked separately.

questions.title: TCP Properties
questions.prompt: A developer of an order service uses TCP so that the server receives the byte stream sent by the client in order. Select one incorrect statement about TCP connections.

choices.text: TCP exchanges byte streams after establishing a connection with the peer.
choices.explanation: It transfers byte streams between the two connected endpoints.

choices.text: If TCP transmission is acknowledged, you can conclude that the order has been successfully registered.
choices.explanation: Acknowledgment of the transfer does not guarantee that the application successfully registered the order.

choices.text: TCP manages ordering and retransmits lost data.
choices.explanation: It delivers an ordered byte stream to the receiving application.

learning.concept: TCP delivery and application processing
learning.reason: TCP establishes a connection and delivers the byte stream in order. The application verifies whether processing by the receiving side succeeded.

questions.title: UDP Responsibilities
questions.prompt: A delivery operator is considering a configuration that uses UDP for live audio. Delayed, old audio has little value, and the behavior when data is missing is determined by the application. Select two incorrect statements about decisions when using UDP.

choices.text: When using UDP, decide where handling of ordering, retransmission, and loss will be performed.
choices.explanation: The application determines the required ordering and behavior when data is missing.

choices.text: UDP always guarantees ordering and retransmission, so no additional design is necessary.
choices.explanation: UDP does not provide those guarantees.

choices.text: Changing the port number provides delivery guarantees.
choices.explanation: A port identifies a service; it does not change delivery guarantees.

choices.text: Because continuing to wait for audio after its playback deadline increases latency, consider a design that allows missing audio.
choices.explanation: For live audio, consider both waiting for expired audio and the impact of missing audio.

learning.concept: Processing handled by the application with UDP
learning.reason: UDP itself does not guarantee delivery, retransmission, or ordering. The application designs how to handle playback deadlines and missing audio.

questions.title: Choosing a Communication Method
questions.prompt: A developer is investigating whether a common communication method can be adopted for live display and file distribution. The impact of missing data and the time available to wait for retransmission differ by use case. Select one incorrect statement about choosing a communication method.

choices.text: For live display and file distribution, decide separately how much loss and retransmission delay can be tolerated.
choices.explanation: The priorities for latency and data integrity differ by use case.

choices.text: Applying TLS automatically resolves loss and ordering, so there is no need to consider the communication method separately.
choices.explanation: Encryption and delivery characteristics are separate. The presence or absence of TLS alone cannot determine whether delivery is suitable for the use case.

choices.text: For file distribution, choose a method that can verify that the received content matches the original data.
choices.explanation: When loss is unacceptable, verify the integrity of the received result.

learning.concept: Selecting communication methods by use case
learning.reason: For each use case, check ordering, loss, and how long retransmission can be awaited. Encryption and delivery characteristics are separate.

questions.title: TLS and HTTP
questions.prompt: A developer checking a connection in a browser receives an HTTP 404 after the TLS handshake completes. Select one conclusion that can be drawn from this result.

choices.text: The TLS connection was established, and the party that returned the HTTP response indicated that the requested resource could not be found.
choices.explanation: Correct. A 404 is an HTTP response, not a TLS failure.

choices.text: The TLS certificate validation failed because there was a 404
choices.explanation: Receiving an HTTP 404 normally means that the TLS stage was completed.

choices.text: Changing only DNS will always resolve the 404
choices.explanation: The cause could be HTTP routing or application resources after DNS succeeds.

learning.concept: TLS establishment and HTTP responses
learning.reason: The TLS connection was established. Because the component returning the HTTP response could not find the requested resource, check the path and delivery configuration.

questions.title: Certificate Validation
questions.prompt: An operations staff member reports that when connecting to orders.example on the order page, the browser displays an error saying that the certificate name does not match. No HTTP response has been received. Select two items to check when validating the TLS certificate.

choices.text: Whether orders.example is included in the certificate’s SAN (Subject Alternative Name).
choices.explanation: Correct. Verify that the connection name matches the certificate name.

choices.text: The certificate’s validity period and trust chain
choices.explanation: Correct. These are conditions for TLS validation.

choices.text: Only the body of the HTTP 404
choices.explanation: Because TLS has not completed, the HTTP body is not useful for diagnosis.

choices.text: Only the application’s JSON response format
choices.explanation: This is not part of the preliminary TLS certificate validation.

learning.concept: Certificate hostname and trust
learning.reason: Match the destination hostname with the certificate’s SAN, and also check the certificate’s validity period and the certificate chain leading to a trusted certificate authority.

questions.title: HTTP Responsibility
questions.prompt: An operations staff member is investigating an order API. The TLS handshake completed successfully, and GET /orders returns HTTP 404. Select one judgment that is incorrect when investigating the cause.

choices.text: Check the HTTP routing of the application or reverse proxy
choices.explanation: 404 is an item to investigate when locating resources at the HTTP layer.

choices.text: Conclude that disabling TLS will guarantee that the HTTP resource is found
choices.explanation: Correct. Disabling TLS will not fix the HTTP path or routing.

choices.text: Record the requested path and HTTP method
choices.explanation: This fixes the reproduction conditions on the HTTP side.

learning.concept: Checking encryption and investigating the application side
learning.reason: Because TLS succeeded, investigate the path and delivery configuration of the layer that returned the HTTP response.

questions.title: Step-by-Step Diagnosis
questions.prompt: A user cannot open the order site orders.example. The operations engineer does not yet know at which stage of communication the problem occurred. Select two pieces of information to use for the initial isolation.

choices.text: The queried name and the IP returned by DNS
choices.explanation: Correct. This fixes the destination for subsequent communication.

choices.text: How far the connection reached among the TCP connection, TLS verification, and HTTP response
choices.explanation: Correct. This narrows down the first stage at which the failure occurred.

choices.text: The result of opening all ports because the cause was unknown
choices.explanation: Opening all ports reduces security and makes the diagnostic evidence ambiguous.

choices.text: Record only whether it succeeded, without recording the name or port
choices.explanation: Without reproduction conditions, you cannot compare the results after a change.

learning.concept: Collecting initial evidence at each communication stage
learning.reason: Clarify the queried name and resolved address, then determine how far the TCP, TLS, and HTTP stages succeeded.

questions.title: Investigating a TCP Rejection
questions.prompt: An operations engineer confirmed that the order API name resolves to the expected IP, but the TCP connection to port 443 is refused. There is no HTTP response. Select two incorrect next investigation approaches.

choices.text: Check whether the destination port is listening and whether the port is allowed
choices.explanation: A refusal is a clue to check service listening status or reachability conditions.

choices.text: Decide that redeploying the HTTP application will definitely solve the problem
choices.explanation: Correct. Evidence from the TCP stage alone does not establish that the HTTP application is the cause.

choices.text: Record the connected IP, port, and source
choices.explanation: This is necessary to observe the same conditions again.

choices.text: Expose all ports to all sources without checking the required scope
choices.explanation: Correct. Abandoning least privilege does not identify the cause.

learning.concept: Investigating the stage at which a TCP connection was refused
learning.reason: Check the destination port’s listening status and the settings along the connection path. Changing HTTP settings or exposing too much cannot identify the cause.

questions.title: Validating the Fix
questions.prompt: The operations engineer changed the security group so that the order site’s EC2 instance can be reached on port 443 from the internal monitoring source. Select two ways to verify the effect of the change and the permitted scope.

choices.text: Retest using the same source, name, port, and request as before the change
choices.explanation: Correct. This keeps the comparison conditions consistent and validates the hypothesis.

choices.text: End the observation without recording anything because it succeeded once
choices.explanation: This does not distinguish an accidental success from a permanent fix.

choices.text: Verify that access is limited to the required sources and ports
choices.explanation: Correct. This confirms that the fix did not create new excessive exposure.

choices.text: Permanently allow all ports because failure is concerning
choices.explanation: This loses least privilege and makes the cause of the incident unclear.

learning.concept: Verifying a change to port access
learning.reason: Use the same source, name, port, and request as before the change, and confirm that only the required connections are allowed.

questions.title: Do Not Confuse the Layers
questions.prompt: An operations engineer confirmed that the name of the ordering site could not be resolved by DNS and that the browser had not obtained the destination IP address. Select the two actions that are incorrect at this point.

choices.text: Record the queried name, the resolver in use, and the error returned.
choices.explanation: This helps clarify the failure at the DNS stage.

choices.text: Conclude that reissuing the TLS certificate will definitely fix the DNS failure.
choices.explanation: Correct. A TLS certificate does not directly fix the cause of DNS resolution.

choices.text: After fixing the DNS configuration, verify the same name resolution again.
choices.explanation: This verifies the result of the fix at the same stage.

choices.text: Conclude that fixing HTTP 404 first will also make name resolution succeed.
choices.explanation: Correct. The process stops at DNS before reaching HTTP.

learning.concept: Troubleshooting when DNS fails
learning.reason: First, investigate the name-resolution configuration and response. Changing TLS or HTTP cannot start the connection if the destination IP is unknown.

units.title: Domains and DNS
units.summary: Treat name resolution, record types, TTL, and TLS/HTTP after DNS as separate responsibilities.
units.objective: Select the query scope and records, estimate the caching impact of TTL, and distinguish post-DNS connectivity from TLS.
explanation: Separate the roles of the Route 53 Resolver, hosted zones, records, TTL, and health checks, and do not confuse successful name resolution with application success.
units.example: Separate name resolution inside and outside the VPC, and design CloudFront aliases, TTL-aware cutovers, and separate TLS and HTTP monitoring.

learningObjectives.text: Explain the query scope of public hosted zones, private hosted zones, and resolvers.
Select A/AAAA, CNAME, or alias records based on the constraints of the destination and name.
Plan a DNS cutover while accounting for TTL and existing caches.
Separate the responsibilities of DNS, TLS, HTTP, and health checks to troubleshoot failures.

sections.title: Until DNS returns the record corresponding to a domain name
paragraphs: DNS queries the record corresponding to a domain name so that users can obtain the destination to connect to. With Route 53 public hosted zones and private hosted zones, the scope reached by a query differs.

For name resolution within a VPC, use Amazon Route 53 VPC Resolver. It resolves VPC-specific names and records in private hosted zones, and also handles queries to public DNS. If name resolution fails, check the query source, hosted zone, DNS delegation, and target record in that order.
A DNS response provides destination information. Even if a response is obtained, the HTTP response, TLS certificate, and application authorization may not all succeed.

example.scenario: An EC2 instance in a VPC cannot resolve api.example.com.
steps: Identify the resolver queried by the EC2 instance and the VPC.
Check the association with the private hosted zone and the record name.
Check the response with dig or a similar tool, and separately verify TCP/TLS after DNS.
example.outcome: Distinguish DNS problems from connection and TLS problems during investigation.

misconception.claim: If a DNS name resolves to an IP address, the web application can always be used.
misconception.correction: DNS only returns the destination. Check HTTP, TLS, security groups, and application authentication separately.

takeaways: Confirm the scope of the resolver and hosted zone.
Verify name resolution and application connectivity separately.
Be aware of the query scope of public DNS and VPC DNS.

sections.title: Choose DNS records that match the destination
paragraphs: An A record maps a name to an IPv4 address, and an AAAA record maps a name to an IPv6 address. A CNAME points to another DNS name, while a Route 53 alias record is used to point a name to a supported AWS resource.

Match the record type to the form of the destination and the name being queried. Also check the restriction that prevents a CNAME from being placed at the zone apex, as well as the restrictions on AWS resources that can be specified by an alias record.
TXT, MX, and CAA records serve purposes other than identifying a Web destination. For a name-resolution problem, compare the expected record type with the actual response.

example.scenario: Point www.example.com to CloudFront.
steps: Check CloudFront's DNS name and whether it is at the zone apex.
In Route 53, choose the corresponding alias A/AAAA record.
Check the response with dig and also check the TLS configuration on the CloudFront side.
example.outcome: Configure the correspondence between an AWS resource and a name with a record that meets the constraints.

misconception.claim: For an AWS resource, place a CNAME on any name.
misconception.correction: Check the zone-apex restriction and the correspondence with the AWS resource, and choose an alias A/AAAA record if necessary.

takeaways: Distinguish the meanings of A/AAAA, CNAME, and alias records.
Check the zone apex and resource restrictions.
Check DNS records and TLS configuration separately.

sections.title: TTL is the time cached responses can be retained
paragraphs: TTL is the number of seconds that a DNS resolver can keep a record response in its cache. Even after a record is changed, an old value may be returned from an existing cache until the previous TTL expires.

Even if TTL is shortened during incident response, values that are already cached do not disappear immediately. Plan the TTL before the switch and operate on the assumption that some users will still receive the old value during the switch.

For alias records, the TTL may be determined by the AWS resource targeted by the routing. Do not confuse the time required for a record change to take effect with the time when the change reaches Route 53.

example.scenario: Switch api.example.com to a new load balancer during incident response.
steps: Check the current TTL and the possible remaining lifetime of cached responses.
Set the switching criteria and the retention period for the old destination.
After the switch, observe responses and application status from multiple resolvers.
example.outcome: You can design the switch and monitoring while accounting for how long old responses may remain.

misconception.claim: If TTL is shortened immediately after changing the record, all users will see the new value.
misconception.correction: Existing caches remain until the old TTL expires. Plan the TTL and waiting time before the switch.

takeaways: TTL is the resolver's cache duration.
Switch on the assumption that old responses will remain after the change.
Also check how the TTL of an alias record is determined.

sections.title: Troubleshoot failures in name resolution and after connection
paragraphs: DNS returns a destination from a name. Whether a TCP connection can be made to that destination, whether HTTP returns the expected response, and whether the TLS certificate matches the name are separate checks.

Route 53 health checks and routing policies affect the selection of DNS responses, but they do not guarantee that all application functions are healthy. Make the monitoring targets and switching conditions explicit.
Diagram the public DNS, private hosted zone, load balancer, CloudFront, and certificate owners to isolate the layer where the failure occurs.

example.scenario: DNS is correct, but users see a certificate error over HTTPS.
steps: Use dig to verify the name and response.
Check the name and validity period of the certificate presented by the destination.
Record HTTP responses, TLS, and DNS as separate monitoring items.
example.outcome: Do not mistake successful DNS for successful TLS or application behavior.

misconception.claim: If the Route 53 health check is healthy, the HTTPS certificate is necessarily correct.
misconception.correction: The health-check conditions and certificate validation are separate. Check DNS, TLS, and HTTP responses individually.

takeaways: DNS is the entry point that returns a destination.
TLS certificates and HTTP responses are separate responsibilities.
Make the monitoring and switching conditions explicit.

questions.title: The role of name resolution
questions.prompt: When a user connects to www.example.com, select two incorrect statements about the role of DNS.

choices.text: Return connection destination information corresponding to a name
choices.explanation: DNS returns record responses based on names.

choices.text: Guarantee the validity of HTTPS certificates
choices.explanation: Verification of TLS certificates is separate from DNS.

choices.text: Complete application authentication
choices.explanation: Authentication is the responsibility of the application.

learning.reason: Verification of TLS certificates is separate from DNS. Authentication is the responsibility of the application.
learning.concept: Confirm the scope of the Resolver and hosted zones.

questions.title: VPC Name Resolution
questions.prompt: A network administrator is evaluating a configuration that allows names registered in a Route 53 private hosted zone to be resolved from EC2 instances within a VPC. Select two of the following configurations that are incorrect.

choices.text: Allow the private hosted zone to be resolved from the entire Internet
choices.explanation: A private hosted zone is used for name resolution within the VPCs associated with it.

choices.text: Verify the association between the querying VPC and the private hosted zone, as well as the record name
choices.explanation: You can verify the zone and name that Resolver can reference.

choices.text: Write IP addresses in every configuration without using DNS
choices.explanation: This makes operational changes and troubleshooting difficult.

learning.reason: A private hosted zone is used for name resolution within the VPCs associated with it. This makes operational changes and troubleshooting difficult.
learning.concept: Verify the scope of Resolver and hosted zones.

questions.title: A and AAAA
questions.prompt: Make web.example.com reachable over both IPv4 and IPv6. Select two combinations of records that are required.

choices.text: An A record for an IPv4 address
choices.explanation: An A record maps to IPv4.

choices.text: An AAAA record for an IPv6 address
choices.explanation: An AAAA record maps to IPv6.

choices.text: Only an MX record for the mail delivery destination
choices.explanation: MX is for a mail delivery destination, not a Web address.

learning.reason: An A record maps to IPv4. An AAAA record maps to IPv6.
learning.concept: Distinguish the meanings of A/AAAA, CNAME, and aliases.

questions.title: Aliases and CNAME
questions.prompt: A DNS administrator directs the apex of the hosted zone, example.com, to an IPv6-enabled CloudFront distribution. The alternate domain name and certificate are already configured on the distribution. Select one incorrect Route 53 configuration.

choices.text: Create a CNAME record at the hosted zone apex that points to the CloudFront domain name.
choices.explanation: A standard CNAME record cannot be created at the hosted zone apex. Use an alias when pointing to CloudFront.

choices.text: For IPv4, create an alias A record that points to the CloudFront distribution.
choices.explanation: A Route 53 alias A record can point from the hosted zone apex to CloudFront.

choices.text: For IPv6, create an alias AAAA record that points to the CloudFront distribution.
choices.explanation: When IPv6 is also provided, configure an alias AAAA record separately from the A record.

learning.reason: CNAME records have restrictions at the zone apex.
learning.concept: Distinguish the meanings of A/AAAA, CNAME, and aliases.

questions.title: Record types
questions.prompt: A DNS administrator wants the subdomain api.example.com to be an alias for api.vendor.example.net, which is managed by another provider. Select one DNS record to use for this purpose.

choices.text: CNAME record
choices.explanation: CNAME points to another DNS name.

choices.text: AAAA record
choices.explanation: AAAA points to an IPv6 address.

choices.text: CAA record
choices.explanation: CAA is used to control certificate issuers.

learning.reason: CNAME points to another DNS name.
learning.concept: Distinguish the meanings of A/AAAA, CNAME, and aliases.

questions.title: Records and TLS
questions.prompt: A web administrator confirmed that the website name resolves to the intended CloudFront distribution, but the browser displays an HTTPS certificate error. Select one setting to check next.

choices.text: Set the TTL to 0 and issue the certificate
choices.explanation: TTL does not fix a certificate name mismatch.

choices.text: Check the name and expiration date of the certificate at the destination, along with the CloudFront-side settings
choices.explanation: This lets you investigate DNS and TLS responsibilities separately.

choices.text: Change the A record to an MX record
choices.explanation: A mail record does not resolve a certificate problem.

learning.reason: This lets you investigate DNS and TLS responsibilities separately.
learning.concept: DNS is the entry point that returns the destination.

questions.title: TTL and propagation
questions.prompt: A DNS administrator changed the destination IP address for api.example.com. The authoritative DNS returns the new value, but some users still connect to the old IP address. Select one possible reason.

choices.text: The resolver may be caching the old response according to the old TTL
choices.explanation: Existing caches remain until the old TTL expires.

choices.text: A DNS change is always reflected immediately for all users
choices.explanation: This ignores the resolver's cache.

choices.text: Changing the TTL immediately deletes existing caches
choices.explanation: The TTL after the change does not clear existing caches.

source.label: Route 53 DNS settings not in effect

learning.reason: Existing caches remain until the old TTL expires.
learning.concept: TTL is the resolver's cache duration.

questions.title: TTL Before Cutover
questions.prompt: An operations team for an online sales site will change the Route 53 DNS record the next day to switch the destination. They want users who are still using old DNS responses to be able to continue connecting. Choose two correct cutover plans.

choices.text: Shorten only the TTL immediately after the cutover.
choices.explanation: Caches using the old TTL remain.

choices.text: Continue running the old destination until caches of old DNS responses expire after the cutover.
choices.explanation: This allows users using old responses to continue connecting.

choices.text: Check the current TTL before the cutover, shorten the TTL, and then wait until caches obtained with the previous longer TTL expire.
choices.explanation: Shortening the TTL first does not immediately change the expiration time of caches stored with the old TTL.

learning.reason: This allows users using old responses to continue connecting. You can design a safe cutover based on caching.
learning.concept: TTL is the resolver's cache duration.

questions.title: Meaning of TTL
questions.prompt: Choose one incorrect statement about what DNS record TTL=300 indicates.

choices.text: Route 53 receives 300 queries.
choices.explanation: TTL is not a count.

choices.text: The resolver can normally cache the response for up to 300 seconds.
choices.explanation: TTL indicates the cache duration in seconds.

choices.text: It is a different value from the HTTP response time.
choices.explanation: TTL indicates the cache duration of a DNS response.

learning.reason: TTL is not a count.
learning.concept: TTL is the resolver's cache duration.

questions.title: DNS and HTTP
questions.prompt: A web operations staff member confirmed that the hostname of an order site resolves to CloudFront as expected. The browser receives HTTP 502 from CloudFront. Choose one incorrect investigation approach at this stage.

choices.text: Review the CloudFront origin settings to verify that the destination hostname, protocol, and port are correct.
choices.explanation: Because the request reached CloudFront from the viewer, investigate the connection conditions from CloudFront to the origin.

choices.text: Recreate the DNS record used by viewers and do not investigate communication from CloudFront to the origin.
choices.explanation: The name used by viewers has already resolved successfully. To investigate the cause of the 502, check the responses from CloudFront and the origin.

choices.text: Record the time of occurrence and the request identifier, then compare the CloudFront response with the origin-side records.
choices.explanation: Following the record for the relevant request helps narrow down whether it reached the destination and which side returned the response.

learning.reason: Name resolution has already succeeded.
learning.concept: DNS is the entry point that returns the destination.

questions.title: Health Check Scope
questions.prompt: Even though the Route 53 health check is healthy, users are receiving TLS errors. Select two things that should be checked.

choices.text: Treat TLS as healthy because DNS is healthy
choices.explanation: DNS responses and certificate validation are separate.

choices.text: Check the health check request content and monitoring conditions
choices.explanation: Identify what the health check is checking.

choices.text: Check the health check conditions and the certificate name, expiration, and TLS settings separately
choices.explanation: This separates the responsibilities of monitoring and TLS.

learning.reason: Identify what the health check is checking. Separate the responsibilities of monitoring and TLS.
learning.concept: DNS is the entry point that returns the destination.

questions.title: Public Boundary
questions.prompt: There are public and private hosted zones with the same name, and you want to return a different destination only inside the VPC. Select two incorrect designs.

choices.text: Expose the private zone to the entire internet
choices.explanation: This contradicts the purpose of a private zone.

choices.text: Maintain a public zone for external users
choices.explanation: Name resolution for external users can continue.

choices.text: Assign a fixed IP to every client
choices.explanation: This loses the management provided by name resolution.

choices.text: Verify the private hosted zone's VPC association and the expected responses inside and outside the VPC
choices.explanation: This allows the query scope to be separated in the design.

learning.reason: This contradicts the purpose of a private zone. The management provided by name resolution is lost.
learning.concept: Verify the scope of the Resolver and hosted zones.

units.title: Designing ranges and available space with CIDR
units.summary: Read CIDR as address ranges and determine range overlap, the number of assignable addresses, and the conditions for communicating with the internet.
units.objective: Plan non-overlapping subnets within a VPC and explain the required capacity and public-access conditions with supporting reasoning.
explanation: CIDR prefixes determine address ranges. Check containment and overlap, AWS-reserved IP addresses, routes, and public IP addresses separately.
units.example: When dividing 10.0.0.0/24 by purpose, consider not only the required capacity but also reserved IP addresses, future growth, and route tables.

learningObjectives.text: Explain the relationship between prefix length and the range of IPv4 addresses.
Determine whether a subnet range fits within the VPC and overlaps with any existing subnets.
Estimate the number of available addresses while accounting for AWS-reserved IP addresses.
Public reachability can be determined from the route and address, rather than the name.

sections.title: The prefix length determines the address range.
paragraphs: In IPv4 CIDR notation, /24 means that the first 24 bits are the network portion. The remaining 8 bits can represent 256 addresses. With /26, 6 bits remain, so it represents 64 addresses. The longer the prefix length, the smaller the address range.

If you divide 10.0.0.0/24 into four equal parts, the boundaries are /26 blocks of 64 addresses each. Verify the start and end of each range: 10.0.0.0/26, 10.0.0.64/26, 10.0.0.128/26, and 10.0.0.192/26.
CIDR is a numerical range, not a name. Before adding a VPC or subnet, verify that it fits within the parent range and does not overlap an existing range.

example.scenario: Divide VPC 10.0.0.0/24 into four subnets of equal size.
steps: Divide the 256 addresses in /24 by 4 to calculate 64 addresses for each subnet.
Assign /26 to each subnet.
List the start and end addresses, and check for gaps and overlaps.
example.outcome: You can validate a subdivision using the range size and boundaries instead of memorizing prefix lengths.

misconception.claim: Because /26 has a larger number than /24, it represents a wider range.
misconception.correction: A prefix length is the length of the network portion. Because /26 has fewer host bits, it represents a narrower range than /24.

takeaways: The longer the prefix length, the smaller the address range.
Verify ranges by their start and end.

sections.title: Keep subnets within the VPC and avoid overlaps
paragraphs: A subnet CIDR must be fully contained within the VPC CIDR and must not overlap another subnet in the same VPC. This condition does not change even when the AZs differ.

In VPC 10.0.0.0/24, which already uses 10.0.0.0/25, 10.0.0.64/26 cannot be added because it is contained in the existing range. In contrast, 10.0.0.128/26 is adjacent to the existing /25 and does not overlap it.
Route tables and subnet names do not eliminate CIDR overlaps. Design the numeric ranges first, then decide the AZ placement and routing.

example.scenario: Create an application subnet in VPC 10.0.0.0/24 in addition to the existing 10.0.0.0/25.
steps: Confirm that the candidate CIDR is within VPC 10.0.0.0/24.
Compare its starting and ending range with the existing /25.
Choose a non-overlapping candidate such as 10.0.0.128/26.
example.outcome: You can determine whether it is valid from CIDR containment and overlap without relying on AZ names or route tables.

misconception.claim: The same CIDR can be reused for two subnets if they are in different AZs.
misconception.correction: Within the same VPC, subnet CIDRs cannot overlap regardless of the AZ.

takeaways: Confirm containment within the parent CIDR first.
Routes cannot resolve overlaps.

sections.title: Subtract AWS-reserved IP addresses when determining capacity
paragraphs: In AWS IPv4 subnets, the first four and the last one, five IP addresses in total, are reserved. Of the 256 addresses in /24, 251 are available for ordinary resources; of the 64 addresses in /26, 59 are available.

Choosing the smallest CIDR based only on the required number of EC2 instances can leave insufficient capacity because of reserved IP addresses and growth. Add together the required number of network interfaces, addresses used by AWS services, and future headroom before choosing the prefix length.
Reserved IP addresses do not change based on route tables or port numbers. Distinguish the available count from the total count and record the assumptions in the design document.

example.scenario: Choose a subnet for a workload that uses up to 50 IPv4 addresses.
steps: Determine that 32 total addresses in /27 are insufficient even before subtracting the reserved addresses.
Subtract the 5 reserved addresses from the 64 total addresses in /26.
Check whether the 59 available addresses provide enough future headroom.
example.outcome: You can plan capacity using the available count without carrying an address shortage into deployment.

misconception.claim: Because /26 has 64 addresses, 64 can always be assigned to EC2 instances.
misconception.correction: In an AWS IPv4 subnet, 5 addresses are reserved, so only 59 are normally available in /26.

takeaways: Total addresses and available addresses are different.
Include reserved IP addresses and growth capacity in the plan.

sections.title: Verify the conditions for external connectivity
paragraphs: Whether a subnet has a route to an internet gateway is determined by the route table association. Public reachability is not determined solely by the CIDR being 10.0.0.0/24 or the subnet being named "public".

To reach an instance from the internet over IPv4, you need a route to an IGW, a public IPv4 address or Elastic IP assigned to the target network interface, and the necessary traffic permitted by security groups or similar controls.

To avoid exposing application or data layers unnecessarily, place only the required entry points on public routes. Design outbound connectivity for private layers separately, using a NAT gateway, VPC endpoint, or another option as required.

example.scenario: An EC2 instance in a subnet named "public" cannot be reached over HTTPS from outside.
steps: In the subnet’s route table, check whether the route with destination 0.0.0.0/0 points to an IGW.
Check whether the EC2 instance has a public IPv4 address or Elastic IP.
Check the minimum required permission for TCP 443 and whether the service is listening.
example.outcome: You can diagnose reachability by separating the route, address, and permission, rather than relying only on the name or CIDR.

misconception.claim: Any instance in a subnet with an IGW route automatically becomes reachable from the internet.
misconception.correction: The instance also needs a public IPv4 address or Elastic IP and the necessary traffic permission.

takeaways: Public reachability is a combination of the route table, address, and permissions.
A subnet name is not evidence of reachability.

questions.title: Prefix and Range
questions.prompt: A network administrator is comparing IPv4 CIDR blocks, 10.0.0.0/24 and 10.0.0.0/26, with the same starting address. Select one correct statement about the relationship between the two address ranges.

choices.text: /26 is a narrower range than /24
choices.explanation: Correct. /26 has 6 host bits and contains 64 addresses.

choices.text: /26 is a broader range than /24
choices.explanation: The longer the prefix length, the narrower the address range.

choices.text: The prefix represents a port number.
choices.explanation: The number after the slash in CIDR is the number of bits in the network portion.

learning.concept: Prefix Length and Range
learning.reason: Because /26 has a network portion that is 2 bits longer than /24, its range is one-quarter the size when they have the same starting address.

questions.title: Four Equal Parts
questions.prompt: A designer wants to divide the 10.0.0.0/24 assigned to a VPC entirely into four non-overlapping subnets of equal size. Select one correct prefix length for each subnet.

choices.explanation: /25 divides it into two equal parts.
Correct. It divides it into four equal parts of 64 addresses each.
It does not divide the range.

learning.concept: Division into Equal Sizes
learning.reason: To divide the /24 address range into four parts, extend the prefix by 2 bits to /26.

questions.title: Calculating the Range
questions.prompt: A designer assigned 10.0.0.0/26 and 10.0.0.64/26 within 10.0.0.0/24. When determining whether the remainder can be used for another subnet, select one incorrect statement about IPv4 CIDR.

choices.text: /24 represents 256 IPv4 addresses
choices.explanation: It is 2 to the 8th power.

choices.text: /26 represents 64 IPv4 addresses
choices.explanation: It is 2 to the 6th power.

choices.text: Two consecutive /26 blocks have the same range as /24
choices.explanation: Two adjacent /26 blocks contain 128 addresses in total. This range corresponds to /25 and does not constitute the entire 256-address /24 range.

learning.concept: Comparing Divided Address Ranges
learning.reason: Combining two adjacent /26 blocks gives 128 addresses, which does not reach the 256 addresses in the entire /24 range.

questions.title: No Overlap
questions.prompt: A network administrator is creating subnets in two Availability Zones of the same VPC. When assigning an IPv4 CIDR to each subnet, select one incorrect statement.

choices.text: Verify that the candidate CIDR is within the VPC CIDR
choices.explanation: A subnet must be contained within the VPC.

choices.text: The same CIDR can be used if the AZs are different
choices.explanation: Correct. Subnet CIDRs within the same VPC cannot overlap, regardless of the AZ.

choices.text: Compare the starting and ending addresses to check for overlap
choices.explanation: Check the numeric ranges.

learning.concept: Availability Zones and address overlap
learning.reason: Even in different Availability Zones, the CIDRs of subnets within the same VPC cannot overlap.

questions.title: Additional Subnets
questions.prompt: A designer is adding a new /26 subnet to the VPC IPv4 CIDR 10.0.0.0/24. 10.0.0.0/25 is already in use. Select two incorrect candidates for the addition.

choices.explanation: Because it is contained in 10.0.0.0/25, it overlaps with the existing subnet.
It is outside the existing /25 and fits within the VPC.
It is outside the existing /25 and fits within the VPC.
It does not fit within the VPC’s 10.0.0.0/24, so it cannot be assigned to this VPC.

learning.concept: Overlap with existing subnets and the VPC range
learning.reason: 10.0.0.64/26 overlaps with the existing range. 10.0.1.0/26 is outside the range assigned to the VPC.

questions.title: Planning Order
questions.prompt: A network administrator is assigning another subnet to a VPC while keeping the existing subnets. Select two conditions that the candidate IPv4 CIDR must satisfy.

choices.text: Be completely contained within the VPC CIDR
choices.explanation: Correct.

choices.text: Not overlap with existing subnets
choices.explanation: Correct.

choices.text: Have a subnet name different from existing names
choices.explanation: A name does not eliminate CIDR overlap.

choices.text: Have a separate route table
choices.explanation: A route table does not determine whether a CIDR is valid.

learning.concept: CIDRs that can be assigned to subnets
learning.reason: Verify that the candidate is completely within the VPC CIDR and does not overlap with existing subnets in the same VPC.

questions.title: Reserved IPs
questions.prompt: A design engineer uses a regular IPv4 /26 subnet with an address range allocated by AWS. Excluding the addresses reserved by AWS, how many IPv4 addresses can be assigned to resources? Select one correct number.

choices.explanation: Five addresses are reserved.
Correct. Subtract the 5 reserved addresses from 64.
Incorrect because the first 4 addresses and the last address are reserved.

learning.concept: Addresses reserved by AWS
learning.reason: Of the 64 addresses in /26, 59 can be assigned after excluding the first 4 and last 1 address reserved by AWS.

questions.title: Capacity Planning
questions.prompt: A platform engineer plans to use up to 50 IPv4 addresses in a subnet. The amount of future growth is uncertain. Select two actions to take before deciding on the size of the new subnet.

choices.text: Add the AWS-reserved IPs to the required number and choose the CIDR
choices.explanation: Correct. Base the decision on the number of usable addresses.

choices.text: Because /27 has 32 addresses, 50 can be used if the reserved addresses are ignored
choices.explanation: There are not enough addresses even in the total.

choices.text: Check the 59 usable addresses in /26 and the available headroom
choices.explanation: Correct.

choices.text: Exclude reserved IPs from the design because they are needed only during communication
choices.explanation: They cannot be assigned, so they must be included in the plan.

learning.concept: Address demand and headroom
learning.reason: Estimate the required range including the addresses reserved by AWS, and verify that there is sufficient headroom beyond the 59 assignable addresses in /26.

questions.title: Handling Reservations
questions.prompt: In an active VPC, an operations engineer is investigating a shortage of IPv4 addresses. Regarding addresses reserved by AWS in a subnet, select one incorrect action.

choices.text: Assign a reserved IP as an EC2 address when addresses are insufficient
choices.explanation: Correct. Reserved IPs generally cannot be assigned to resources.

choices.text: Estimate the required CIDR including the number of reserved IPs
choices.explanation: This allows the number of usable addresses to be determined correctly.

choices.text: The number of reserved addresses affects CIDR capacity planning
choices.explanation: They reduce the number of usable addresses.

learning.concept: Planning when addresses are insufficient
learning.reason: Addresses reserved by AWS cannot be assigned to regular EC2 instances. Consider another subnet or placement that meets the required number of addresses.

questions.title: Public Access Requirements
questions.prompt: A web administrator accepts direct HTTPS connections over IPv4 from users on the internet to EC2. Application listening and communication permissions are already configured. Select two required address and routing conditions.

choices.text: The subnet route table has an outbound route to the IGW
choices.explanation: Correct. The IGW is the route target.

choices.text: EC2 has a public IPv4 address or an Elastic IP
choices.explanation: Correct. This is required for IPv4 reachability through the IGW.

choices.text: The subnet name is public
choices.explanation: A name does not determine reachability.

choices.text: The CIDR is 10.0.0.0/24
choices.explanation: The CIDR numbers alone do not determine public accessibility.

learning.concept: Addresses and routes required for direct connectivity
learning.reason: Verify that EC2 has a public IPv4 address or an Elastic IP and that an outbound route to the internet gateway exists.

questions.title: Investigating Inability to Access Publicly
questions.prompt: An operations administrator is investigating why an internet user cannot connect via HTTPS to a web application on EC2 with a public IPv4 address. Select two incorrect investigation approaches.

choices.text: Check the IGW route in the relevant route table
choices.explanation: This verifies the reachability conditions.

choices.text: Do not check the route table because the subnet name is public
choices.explanation: Correct. The name is not evidence.

choices.text: Check permission for port 443 and the service listener
