questions.prompt: The person responsible for updating a payment API first sends some production requests to the updated version and validates the results. Select one correct description of this method.

choices.text: As a canary deployment, process the remaining requests using the currently running version
choices.explanation: You can verify the results of the updated version while keeping the initial release scope limited.

choices.text: Stop all instances of the currently running version before releasing the updated version
choices.explanation: Stopping the currently running version means the remaining requests cannot be processed.

choices.text: With a rolling update, always replace all tasks simultaneously
choices.explanation: With a rolling update, tasks are replaced sequentially.

source.label: Amazon ECS deployment controllers and strategies

learning.reason: You can verify the results of the updated version while keeping the initial release scope limited.
learning.concept: Distinguish replacing tasks from switching where user traffic is sent.

questions.title: Switching between two environments
questions.prompt: The operator of a reservations API runs the current environment alongside the updated environment and switches user traffic to the updated environment after validation. Select one incorrect description of blue/green deployments.

choices.text: You can validate the new environment before switching users
choices.explanation: You can prepare the new environment while keeping the current environment running.

choices.text: Check the capacity of the two environments running simultaneously
choices.explanation: You need enough capacity to run both environments temporarily.

choices.text: Switching users back automatically reverts changes to shared data
choices.explanation: Switching traffic back does not change the data.

source.label: Amazon ECS deployment controllers and strategies

learning.reason: Switching traffic back does not change the data.
learning.concept: Distinguish replacing tasks from switching where user traffic is sent.

questions.title: Choose a release method based on requirements
questions.prompt: The operations team for a reservations API can use temporary additional capacity but wants to limit the impact on users if a new feature behaves abnormally. Select two actions to take when choosing a method.

choices.text: Determine the percentage of requests to send to the updated version first
choices.explanation: This is a condition for choosing a method that can limit the impact.

choices.text: Do not investigate compatibility even when the previous and updated versions use the same data
choices.explanation: Compatibility of shared data is necessary regardless of the method.

choices.text: Even without monitoring, switch all users at once
choices.explanation: Detecting abnormalities and limiting their impact becomes more difficult.

choices.text: Confirm the capacity for running environments in parallel and the rollback procedure
choices.explanation: This allows you to assess whether a method that switches between environments is feasible.

choices.text: Assume that choosing a method enables automatic recovery from every failure
choices.explanation: Problems with data or external dependencies must be checked separately.

source.label: Amazon ECS deployment controllers and strategies

learning.reason: This is a condition for choosing a method that can limit the impact. This allows you to assess whether a method that switches between environments is feasible.
learning.concept: Distinguish replacing tasks from switching where user traffic is sent.

questions.title: Abort conditions to decide before release
questions.prompt: The person responsible for the Search API is releasing an updated version to some production requests. To detect abnormalities caused by the updated version early, select two things that should be decided before release.

choices.text: The observation period and the error-rate or response-time thresholds for stopping the rollout
choices.explanation: This allows the team to agree in advance on how to evaluate the metrics.

choices.text: A policy to release the updated version to everyone at the scheduled time even if abnormalities occur
choices.explanation: The defined safety conditions must take precedence over the release time.

choices.text: The operations and metrics to compare between the updated and previous versions
choices.explanation: This makes it possible to see differences for the same operation, making failures in the updated version less likely to be missed than when looking only at overall averages.

source.label: Configuring alarms and rollback for AWS CodeDeploy

learning.reason: This allows the team to agree in advance on how to evaluate the metrics. It also makes it possible to see differences for the same operation, making failures in the updated version less likely to be missed than when looking only at overall averages.
learning.concept: Decide the monitoring items, observation period, and abort conditions before release.

questions.title: When monitoring data is insufficient
questions.prompt: After releasing an updated version of the Orders API to only 5%, the metric for the updated version’s order-completion rate became unavailable. Select two judgments by the person responsible that are incorrect.

choices.text: Do not expand the switch to the updated version until the order-completion rate can be verified
choices.explanation: This avoids expanding the scope without the necessary monitoring and maintains the safety conditions.

choices.text: Conclude that no failure has occurred because the metrics cannot be retrieved
choices.explanation: Measurement may have stopped, and the inability to retrieve metrics is not evidence of normal operation.

choices.text: Look only at the combined total count for the previous and updated versions, then switch the remaining traffic
choices.explanation: The updated version’s order-completion rate cannot be verified from the total count alone.

source.label: Configuring alarms and rollback for AWS CodeDeploy

learning.reason: Measurement may have stopped, and the inability to retrieve metrics is not evidence of normal operation. The updated version’s order-completion rate cannot be verified from the total count alone.
learning.concept: Decide the monitoring items, observation period, and abort conditions before release.

questions.title: Failures hidden by the overall average
questions.prompt: The updated version of the Delivery API is processing part of the production traffic. The API’s overall average response time is stable, but delivery-registration failures have increased only for the updated version. Select two judgments that are incorrect in this situation.

choices.text: Separately check the delivery-registration success rates for the updated and previous versions
choices.explanation: This makes it possible to find failures in processing that affect users.

choices.text: Conclude that there is no abnormality because the overall average is stable
choices.explanation: Failures limited to one part cannot be detected from the overall average.

choices.text: Stop switching to the updated version if the failures meet the abort conditions
choices.explanation: This makes it possible to investigate the cause without expanding the scope of the impact.

choices.text: Have the person responsible check the recovery procedure and the time when the abnormality began
choices.explanation: This helps with recovery decisions and subsequent investigation.

choices.text: Exclude failed operations and continue the release until the success rate returns
choices.explanation: Excluding failures from the aggregation hides their impact on users.

source.label: Configuring alarms and rollback for AWS CodeDeploy

learning.reason: Failures limited to one part cannot be detected from the overall average. Excluding failures from the aggregation hides their impact on users.
learning.concept: Decide the monitoring items, observation period, and abort conditions before release.

questions.title: Meaning of rollback
questions.prompt: The updated version of the Inventory API caused a failure. It has been confirmed that the current data can be read using the previous version. Select one operation that constitutes a rollback.

choices.text: Redeploy the application from before the failure
choices.explanation: This operation returns to the previous execution configuration.

choices.text: Deploy fixes while keeping the current version
choices.explanation: This is a way to release a corrected version, not an operation that returns to the previous version.

choices.text: Delete the error logs
choices.explanation: The application version remains unchanged, and the failure is not resolved.

learning.reason: This operation returns to the previous execution configuration.
learning.concept: Before applying the previous version, examine its compatibility with the data and dependencies.

questions.title: Data does not change during a rollback
questions.prompt: The updated version of the Reservations API wrote some reservations in a format that the previous version cannot read. When choosing a recovery method, select the one incorrect judgment.

choices.text: Verify whether the previous version can handle the new reservations
choices.explanation: The condition for rolling back is that the previous version can read the current data.

choices.text: Also compare recovery using a corrected version that can handle the new format
choices.explanation: This is an alternative recovery method to consider when returning to the previous version is not possible.

choices.text: If traffic is returned to the previous version, the reservation contents will automatically revert as well
choices.explanation: Returning traffic does not restore data that has already been saved.

learning.reason: Returning traffic does not restore data that has already been saved.
learning.concept: Before applying the previous version, examine its compatibility with the data and dependencies.

questions.title: Verify the service after a rollback
questions.prompt: The Orders API, which showed an anomaly in charge calculation, was rolled back to the previous version. Select two procedures that the operations team should use to confirm that the impact on users has been resolved.

choices.text: Verify that actual order creation and lookup succeed
choices.explanation: This confirms that the operations required for business have been restored.

choices.text: Judge that recovery is complete just because the switch has finished
choices.explanation: It is necessary to separately verify that processing has actually been restored.

choices.text: Delete all orders from during the failure
choices.explanation: Deleting orders without determining whether they are unprocessed or duplicates could result in the loss of valid orders.

choices.text: Distinguish orders saved during the failure from orders that should be reprocessed
choices.explanation: This confirms the scope of the impact that the deployment rollback has on the data.

choices.text: Do not check monitoring metrics because the previous version has been restored
choices.explanation: Even the previous version may not operate without problems in the current environment.

learning.reason: This confirms that the operations required for business have been restored. This confirms the scope of the impact that the deployment rollback has on the data.
learning.concept: Before applying the previous version, examine its compatibility with the data and dependencies.

questions.title: Keep columns usable by both old and new versions
questions.prompt: A person responsible for the membership API renames a column in member data while running the previous and updated versions side by side. Select one safe procedure.

choices.text: Add the new column and keep the old column available during the migration period.
choices.explanation: The data can be handled even while the old and new applications run simultaneously.

choices.text: Delete the old column first, and then deploy the updated version.
choices.explanation: During the migration, the previous version cannot use the old column, causing processing to fail.

choices.text: Delete the old column without confirming that data migration is complete.
choices.explanation: If any data is missed during migration, values could be lost.

source.label: AWS Prescriptive Guidance: Database Schema Changes

learning.reason: The data can be handled even while the old and new applications run simultaneously.
learning.concept: Add and migrate first, then remove the old structure after the previous version is no longer needed.

questions.title: Orders placed after the backup
questions.prompt: You are restoring an order database from a backup to another environment. Orders were also placed after the backup was taken. Select one judgment by the operations staff that is incorrect.

choices.text: Identify the orders placed after the backup was taken.
choices.explanation: You can understand which changes might be lost after restoration.

choices.text: Because the restoration succeeded, assume that it includes all orders placed afterward.
choices.explanation: Changes made after the restoration point are not necessarily included.

choices.text: Compare the old and new order data and determine which differences should be applied to the restoration target.
choices.explanation: Before the switchover, you can identify items requiring handling for omissions, duplicates, and reprocessing.

source.label: AWS Prescriptive Guidance: Database Schema Changes

learning.reason: Changes made after the restoration point are not necessarily included.
learning.concept: Add and migrate first, then remove the old structure after the previous version is no longer needed.

questions.title: Distinguish application recovery from data recovery
questions.prompt: An updated version of a reservation API also changes the data structure. The operations team is planning how far back the application and data can be restored during a failure. Select two incorrect ideas.

choices.text: Verify whether the previous version can read data written by the updated version.
choices.explanation: This verification is necessary to roll back the application.

choices.text: Assume that applying the previous version automatically reverts the schema changes as well.
choices.explanation: Deploying an application does not revert the database structure.

choices.text: Prepare a restoration target and verify that the application can use the restored data.
choices.explanation: You can verify that the combination of the data and application works.

choices.text: When restoring from a backup, decide how to handle new reservations created after the backup was taken.
choices.explanation: Data created after the restoration point may be lost.

choices.text: Because the backup was created successfully, skip validating the restoration procedure.
choices.explanation: The existence of a backup alone does not confirm the restoration procedure or the time required.

source.label: AWS Prescriptive Guidance: Database Schema Changes

learning.reason: Deploying an application does not revert the database structure. The existence of a backup alone does not confirm the restoration procedure or the time required.
learning.concept: Add and migrate first, then remove the old structure after the previous version is no longer needed.

units.title: Monitoring and Improvement
units.summary: Using the Orders API as an example, learn how to read metrics, investigate the causes of incidents, and verify the effectiveness of countermeasures.
units.objective: You can explain how to use metrics, logs, and traces appropriately, as well as how to define service quality goals and investigate incidents.
explanation: Monitoring is used to detect anomalies, investigate their causes, and verify changes afterward. Through the Orders API example, you will learn which data to examine in each situation.
units.example: When the Orders API becomes slow, find anomalies in the response-time graph and investigate possible causes using logs and traces.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish what metrics, logs, and traces can tell you.
You can examine latency, errors, request volume, and throughput to investigate the impact on users and possible causes.
You can define the metrics, target values, aggregation period, and the procedure to follow when you receive an alert.
You can form hypotheses about the causes of incidents, test them, and compare the impact on users before and after a change.

sections.title: Find anomalies and trace a single transaction
paragraphs: When the Orders API is slow, first look at the response-time metrics. Metrics are values recorded over time. They help narrow down when the anomaly started and which operation is showing symptoms.
Logs retain errors and request IDs, among other details, for what happened at that time. A trace shows which services a single request passed through and how long each operation took.

First narrow the scope with metrics, then check the logs and traces from the same time period. Making timestamps, request IDs, and trace IDs trackable makes it easier to correlate different types of data.

example.scenario: A person monitoring the Orders API noticed around noon that the time required to complete a purchase had increased.
steps: Review the response time for each operation and confirm that only order registration became slow.
Examine the logs from the same time period to find the IDs of failed requests and the error details.
Open the trace for a slow request and check which call took the most time.
example.outcome: The call to the inventory service was taking a long time. The investigation can be narrowed to the inventory service and its dependencies.

misconception.claim: You can determine the cause of a slow single request by looking at the API's overall average response time.
misconception.correction: The average response time shows changes across the whole system. To understand the details of a single request, examine the trace for that request.

takeaways: Use metrics to narrow the scope of an anomaly.
Logs show individual events, while traces show the processing path of a single request.

sections.title: Observing latency, errors, load, and capacity
paragraphs: Looking at a service from four perspectives makes it easier to choose where to start an investigation. Latency is the time users wait, errors are failed operations, traffic is the volume of requests received, and saturation indicates how close processing capacity is to its limit.

Even when average latency does not change, some requests may become much slower. p95 is an approximate measure indicating that about 95% of measured requests completed within that time. Compare the same API operation over periods of the same length and in the same units.

If a queue is growing, processing capacity may be insufficient. The fact that CPU utilization and errors increased at the same time does not identify the cause. Check request volume and the state of dependencies, and investigate whether another cause exists.

example.scenario: An order API operator confirmed that latency and HTTP 5xx errors were increasing during the lunch break.
steps: Line up the order-registration p95 latency, error rate, and request count for the same time period.
Check not only CPU utilization, but also the number of items waiting for processing and database connection wait time.
Keep the increase in request count and latency in dependent services as candidate causes, and investigate them using logs and traces.
example.outcome: You can explain separately the impact on users and the candidate causes.

misconception.claim: If CPU utilization and the error rate increase at the same time, you can conclude that CPU is the cause.
misconception.correction: One change may have affected both. Also investigate request volume during the same period and the processing time of each service.

takeaways: Measure the impact on users with latency and errors.
Changes in request volume and saturation provide clues for investigating the cause.

sections.title: Defining quality metrics and objectives
paragraphs: A service-level indicator (SLI) is a value used to measure service quality. For an order API, the proportion of order requests that succeed within 500 milliseconds can be used as an indicator. First define which requests are in scope and what counts as success.

A service-level objective (SLO) is the target you want to achieve for that indicator. For example, “At least 99.9% of order requests in the most recent 28 days succeed within 500 milliseconds.” In CloudWatch, a method with a moving evaluation period such as the most recent 28 days is called a rolling interval.

CloudWatch has request-based SLOs and time-based SLOs. In this order API example, each request is evaluated individually. For a time-based SLO, you might examine how much of one day consisted of one-minute periods that met the target. One day is the evaluation period, and one minute is the evaluation interval. Also define alert notification conditions and owners. If metrics cannot be retrieved, use logs or other telemetry to determine whether there were no requests or measurement stopped.

example.scenario: The order API operations team decided to measure how long users were kept waiting during purchases.
steps: Count the requests received by the order-registration API as the evaluation population.
Divide the number that succeeded within 500 milliseconds by the total number in the evaluation population.
Set the target for the most recent 28 days to at least 99.9%, and define the procedure for checking when data does not arrive.
example.outcome: Even if the person in charge changes, anyone can verify target attainment using the same conditions.

misconception.claim: If metrics do not appear on the monitoring screen, there was no incident during that period.
misconception.correction: Metrics may be absent both when there were no requests and when the measurement mechanism stopped. Check separately aggregated request counts and whether the measurement process is running.

takeaways: An SLI is the value measured; an SLO is the target you want to achieve for that value.
Specify the evaluation period and operations in scope, and define the procedure to follow after an alert.

sections.title: Forming hypotheses about causes and measuring the effect of mitigations
paragraphs: When investigating an incident, record when it occurred, which operation was involved, and who was affected. Also check the deployment immediately beforehand and changes in request volume, and separate established facts from candidate causes.

Suppose the order API is slow and RDS Proxy DatabaseConnectionsBorrowLatency has increased. Assume that the connection pool has no available capacity and change the configuration in some environments. Examining how this metric changes can test the hypothesis.

When evaluating a mitigation, keep conditions such as the operation in scope, the evaluation period, and load consistent before and after the change. Do not rely only on internal metrics; also compare latency and error rate to confirm whether the impact on users improved.

example.scenario: An operator believes the order API became slow because it is waiting for an available database connection.
steps: Measure connection wait time, latency, and error rate under a similar load.
Change only the connection-pool configuration in some environments, and also observe the load on the database side.
Compare the values and traces before and after the change over evaluation periods of the same length, and record the results and what remains unknown.
example.outcome: If connection wait time and user wait time decrease without worsening the error rate, this provides a basis for deciding whether to expand the configuration change.

misconception.claim: If changing the configuration lowers CPU utilization, you can conclude that the impact on users also improved.
misconception.correction: CPU utilization is an internal-state value. Compare the time users waited and the proportion of failed operations under the same conditions.

takeaways: Test hypotheses within a limited scope.
Compare before and after under the same conditions and confirm whether users experienced an improvement.

questions.title: Metrics used for monitoring
questions.prompt: An operator responsible for the order API compares graphs to determine whether the load changed between yesterday and today. Select one appropriate monitoring metric.

choices.text: The number of requests per minute
choices.explanation: Plotting values measured at the same interval reveals changes in load.

choices.text: The order of services through which one order passed
choices.explanation: The path of a single request is recorded in a trace.

choices.text: An exception message produced by a request
choices.explanation: Information that records a specific event is handled as a log.

learning.reason: Plotting values measured at the same interval reveals changes in load.
learning.concept: Narrow down the scope of anomalies with metrics.

questions.title: Identifying slow calls
questions.prompt: The order API is slow, and an operator investigates which dependent service call took time for one order. Select one appropriate type of data.

choices.text: The average CPU utilization of the API server
choices.explanation: CPU utilization does not show the time spent by each destination for a specific request.

choices.text: The start time and processing time for each call recorded in the request trace
choices.explanation: You can follow the target request and determine what was slow at each service.

choices.text: The response-time target set by the team
choices.explanation: A target value is a quality standard, not a record of the actual call time.

learning.reason: You can follow the target request and determine what was slow at each service.
learning.concept: Narrow down the scope of anomalies with metrics.

questions.title: From Anomalous Times to Logs and Traces
questions.prompt: Errors are occurring intermittently in the order API. Select one appropriate procedure for narrowing down the time period of the anomaly and tracing the failed requests.

choices.text: Determine the cause of all failures based only on the first log line found.
choices.explanation: A single record does not reveal the scope of the issue or other possible causes.

choices.text: Estimate the total number of requests for the entire day from one trace and end the investigation.
choices.explanation: One trace does not indicate the total number of requests.

choices.text: View the error rate by hour, then correlate the logs and traces from that time period.
choices.explanation: Use metrics to narrow the scope, then investigate the cause using individual data from the same time period.

learning.reason: Use metrics to narrow the scope, then investigate the cause using individual data from the same time period.
learning.concept: Narrow down the scope of anomalies using metrics.

questions.title: The Role of the Four Perspectives
questions.prompt: The operations team for an order API selected latency, errors, traffic, and saturation as monitoring items. Select one incorrect description of their respective roles.

choices.text: Latency indicates the time taken to process a request.
choices.explanation: This metric captures the time users spend waiting.

choices.text: For errors, examine the number of failed operations and the failure rate.
choices.explanation: Both the number of failures and the failure rate are metrics for observing errors.

choices.text: For traffic, examine the volume of requests received during a given period.
choices.explanation: This helps you understand the load placed on the service.

choices.text: Saturation refers to the proportion of successful HTTP requests.
choices.explanation: Saturation indicates how close CPU or processing capacity is to its limit. Success rate is calculated separately.

learning.reason: Saturation indicates how close CPU or processing capacity is to its limit. Success rate is calculated separately.
learning.concept: Measure the impact on users through latency and errors.

questions.title: The Relationship Between CPU Utilization and Errors
questions.prompt: During the day, the order API showed simultaneous increases in CPU utilization and the number of HTTP 5xx errors. Select one incorrect initial response for investigating the cause.

choices.text: Conclude that the increase in CPU utilization is the cause and do not check any other metrics.
choices.explanation: An increase in request volume or another factor may have caused both.

choices.text: Check the number of requests during the same period and latency by operation.
choices.explanation: This allows you to check changes in load and the operations that were affected.

choices.text: Use logs and traces to investigate errors or timeouts in dependencies.
choices.explanation: This provides information for determining whether another cause exists.

learning.reason: An increase in request volume or another factor may have caused both.
learning.concept: Measure the impact on users through latency and errors.

questions.title: Analyzing Some Slow Requests
questions.prompt: The average response time for the order API is about the same as last week, but some users have reported that it is slow. Choose two ways for the person in charge to investigate the impact and cause.

choices.text: Conclude that there are no slow requests because the average response time has not changed
choices.explanation: Some substantial delays may not be visible from the average alone.

choices.text: Compare the p95 response times over aggregation periods of the same length for the same API operation
choices.explanation: Using the same comparison conditions makes it possible to track changes in the slower requests.

choices.text: Estimate the response time from CPU utilization and do not measure the actual response time
choices.explanation: Internal resource utilization alone cannot identify how long users waited.

choices.text: Directly compare p95 values for different operations or aggregation periods
choices.explanation: Differences in comparison conditions may appear to be differences in the values.

choices.text: Also check the number of requests and the number of items waiting for processing during the same time period
choices.explanation: This helps determine whether load or processing capacity could be a cause.

learning.reason: Using the same comparison conditions makes it possible to track changes in the slower requests. This helps determine whether load or processing capacity could be a cause.
learning.concept: Measure the impact on users using response times and errors.

questions.title: Order API Success Rate
questions.prompt: The order API operations team uses the proportion of requests that succeeded within 500 milliseconds as the SLI. Choose two correct elements of the calculation.

choices.text: The numerator is the number of target requests that succeeded within 500 milliseconds
choices.explanation: The numerator includes the number of requests that met the condition for being counted as successful.

choices.text: The denominator is the total number of requests that reached the operation being measured
choices.explanation: The denominator is the entire target population, including both successes and failures.

choices.text: A denominator is unnecessary; the proportion can be calculated from the number of successful requests alone
choices.explanation: A total number to compare against is required to calculate a proportion.

learning.reason: The numerator includes the number of requests that met the condition for being counted as successful. The denominator is the entire target population, including both successes and failures.
learning.concept: An SLI is a value to measure, while an SLO is the target to achieve for that value.

questions.title: Periods When Metrics Cannot Be Retrieved
questions.prompt: A person monitoring the order API success rate notices that metrics cannot be retrieved during a particular period. Choose one incorrect way to handle this period.

choices.text: Investigate whether no order requests arrived or the measurement process stopped
choices.explanation: Either situation could result in metrics not being retrievable.

choices.text: Treat the period when metrics cannot be retrieved as normal and do not check the cause
choices.explanation: If measurement has stopped, this approach will leave the problem unnoticed.

choices.text: Check the number of requests aggregated through another path and the operating status of the measurement process
choices.explanation: Separating the observation paths makes it possible to distinguish between a state in which there are no requests and a state in which measurement has stopped.

learning.reason: If measurement has stopped, this approach will leave the problem unnoticed.
learning.concept: An SLI is a value to measure, while an SLO is the target to achieve for that value.

questions.title: Designing SLOs and alerts
questions.prompt: The operations team for the Orders API configures an SLO in CloudWatch that classifies each target request as successful or failed and evaluates the success rate. An alert notifies the team when operator action is required. Select two appropriate actions for this design.

choices.text: Define the API operations in scope, the conditions for counting a request as successful, the target value, and the aggregation period.
choices.explanation: This clarifies which results from which operations are counted and which period’s results are compared with the target.

choices.text: Treat calendar months and the most recent 28 days as results from the same range without distinguishing them.
choices.explanation: Calendar months and the most recent 28 days differ in the period and length being evaluated.

choices.text: Issue notifications, but do not decide what the recipient should check.
choices.explanation: Define contacts and verification procedures so that the operator can take action.

choices.text: Define how to handle missing data and what to check after a notification.
choices.explanation: This prevents missed measurement stoppages and helps the operator decide the next action.

choices.text: Determine the success rate using only the number of successful requests without defining the total number of target requests.
choices.explanation: Define the entire number of requests in scope so that the success rate can be calculated.

learning.reason: Define the target operations and success conditions, and compare the success rate during the evaluation period with the target. Also define how to respond when data is missing or a notification is received.
learning.concept: An SLI is the value being measured, while an SLO is the target you want to achieve for that value.

questions.title: Testing an incident hypothesis
questions.prompt: Intermittent timeouts are occurring in the Orders API. When investigating the cause of the incident, select two incorrect actions.

choices.text: Record the occurrence time, target operation, impact on users, and changes made immediately beforehand.
choices.explanation: You can later check logs and metrics under the same conditions.

choices.text: Conclude that a single metric is the cause as soon as it changes at the same time.
choices.explanation: A simultaneous change alone does not show the relationship between cause and effect.

choices.text: Develop candidate causes from the observed data and system configuration.
choices.explanation: This links possible causes with the data to check next.

choices.text: Consider what would be recorded if each candidate were correct, then compare it with logs and traces.
choices.explanation: You can compare candidate causes using evidence.

choices.text: Exclude results that do not fit the initial assessment and do not revisit the candidate causes.
choices.explanation: Results that do not fit the assessment are also material for revising the hypothesis.

learning.reason: A simultaneous change alone does not show the relationship between cause and effect. Results that do not fit the assessment are also material for revising the hypothesis.
learning.concept: Test hypotheses by narrowing their scope.

questions.title: Testing the database connection pool
questions.prompt: The Orders API connects to Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL through Amazon RDS Proxy. Order confirmation has become slower, and the operations team suspects the time RDS Proxy takes to lend out a database connection. When changing the connection pool configuration in some environments, select two incorrect ways to verify the effect.

choices.text: Conclude that user wait time also decreased solely because CPU utilization decreased.
choices.explanation: Measure the time users waited and the error rate to confirm the actual impact.

choices.text: Before and after the change, compare response time and error rate while keeping the target operation, aggregation-period length, and load the same.
choices.explanation: Keeping comparison conditions consistent makes it easier to examine the impact of the change.

choices.text: Compare RDS Proxy’s DatabaseConnectionsBorrowLatency before and after the change to determine whether the time the proxy takes to obtain a database connection decreased.
choices.explanation: This metric shows in microseconds how long RDS Proxy took to obtain a database connection. Measure the Orders API response time separately.

choices.text: Change the configuration in all environments at once based only on the fact that connection waits and delayed responses occurred simultaneously.
choices.explanation: A simultaneous change alone cannot establish the cause. Testing in some environments limits the impact.

choices.text: Record the conditions of the change, the results, and what is still unknown.
choices.explanation: This allows the basis for the decision to be checked later and the same conditions to be reproduced in a subsequent investigation.

learning.concept: Time spent waiting for a connection and Orders API response time
learning.reason: Investigate the wait time on the connection-pool side and also check whether user response times and errors improved under the same load and operations.

questions.title: Evaluating CPU load mitigation
questions.prompt: The person responsible for the Orders API notices that both the number of HTTP 5xx errors and CPU utilization have increased. Choose two incorrect responses regarding investigating the cause and confirming the effectiveness of the mitigation.

choices.text: Check the request volume, the status of dependencies, and traces for the relevant operations to narrow down possible causes.
choices.explanation: Comparing multiple data points helps validate possible causes.

choices.text: For the same API operation, compare the error rate and response time before and after the change under equivalent conditions.
choices.explanation: This confirms whether the impact on users has improved.

choices.text: Treat CPU load as the sole cause simply because CPU utilization and 5xx errors increased during the same period.
choices.explanation: Other factors, such as request volume, may have affected both.

choices.text: Test the mitigation in part of the environment and measure whether the change reduces the anomalies.
choices.explanation: This makes it possible to investigate whether the mitigation worked while limiting the impact.

choices.text: Directly compare the SLO attainment rates before and after the change even when the aggregation periods or API operations differ.
choices.explanation: When the periods or operations differ, the requests being evaluated also change, making it difficult to determine whether the difference resulted from the mitigation.

learning.reason: Other factors, such as request volume, may have affected both. Differences in aggregation conditions may appear as differences in attainment rates.
learning.concept: Test hypotheses by narrowing their scope.
